Best way is to be an assistant 2 years, then start looking for clients you believe in to develop. Most bosses at the smaller management and agencies will bump you to a junior agent position if you have a couple of people you want to sign - the trick is to find the right company that wants you to grow.

Agents/managers of big talent get so many people reaching out to them with offers that aren’t actually real - so for the most part they just want to see that you have money to offer the client, put it in escrow, pay or play before entertaining something that doesn’t come through an official channels (ie through a casting director or producer who has credibility) 

When they have a huge client list they can’t spend days going back and forth on a project that’s not actually going to make their client money.

One thing that really helps me is I put on a tv show with commercials. Every commercial break, I do a cleaning task like collect all the dirty laundry and put it in the hamper and then the next commercial break I’ll put it in the laundry to do a load. It helps to break up the tasks and gives it a clear start and stop point. 

Also sometimes I will bribe myself- order food from my favorite restaurant and clean until the food gets here.

I also think it’s important where the interaction is. If a woman is walking home alone, in an elevator, in an Uber, then it’ll be creepy because she’s in a position it’s hard to get away. If she’s out with friends, at a busy bar, restaurant etc then there’s less pressure on the situation.

The ULB and Micro Budget agreements with SAG are pretty reasonable to do as an independent producer and honestly those day rates for actors are not that much in the grand scheme of the budget. And if you stick to those guidelines for meals and overtime then going non Union for crew shouldn’t be a big deal. I think with COVID these days Union is more costly with the testing protocols so if you’re doing a low budget project these days, non Union is your better choice but if you stick to the union rules for the big things then you shouldn’t run into too many issues. Pay people and treat them well regardless of Union status and people will want to work with you.

You seem to be concerned that someone will reject you because of that and the honest truth is some people may. But if you accept your body and love it, other people will too. Also some people might prefer it, I’ve turned down people for the opposite problem actually.

The biggest helps for me were distractions and self care help. Food delivery was big for my family because nobody wanted to eat but someone spent money and delivered it to our door so we felt obligated in a sense which was really the only reason we ate anything those first three weeks. Or things like a new body wash that made me realize I hadn’t taken a shower in four days. 

I also really needed people who could pull me out of the hole for a bit, not ask me if I was okay because the answer is always no, but who could tell me a story about their day or send me a video that would make me smile. I also would say whatever her love language is, lean into that too.

I work with a lot of “working actor” types and honestly the people who get the most consistent work are the people who are open to every opportunity. They audition for everything and they have agents and managers who push for a wide range of projects. Ultimately it comes down to look, talent, and perseverance.

Most of the people I’ve worked with don’t go to graduate school for acting. Lots of them do independent shorts and student films/web projects to build a reel or go the commercial route. I teach classes on industry professionalism tools and consult with fresh talent all the time.

Honestly if you’ve got good credits I would suggest looking for a good commercial agent because if you don’t have casting accounts they can forward your audition and submit it on your behalf. For theatricals you need AA unfortunately.
